reference.source: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
clinicalPearls: Combines unilateral weakness and sensory loss of the face, arm and leg without cortical signs, classically from a lacune at the junction of the thalamus and adjacent posterior internal capsule.
The lesion typically involves thalamocapsular territory supplied by penetrating arteries, interrupting both ascending sensory relay and descending corticospinal fibres.
Absence of aphasia, neglect, hemianopia and gaze palsy distinguishes it from a large middle cerebral artery cortical infarct.
It is one of the classical Fisher lacunar syndromes and shares hypertensive small-vessel pathology with the pure motor and pure sensory variants.
A comparable clinical picture can arise from a small primary intracerebral haemorrhage in the same region, so imaging is essential.
Diffusion-weighted MRI reliably localises the small deep infarct when CT is unrevealing.
Because the deficit is 'complete' across motor and sensory domains, functional impact can exceed that of the single-modality lacunar syndromes.
Secondary prevention rests on blood pressure, glycaemic and lipid control together with antiplatelet therapy.
reference.pathophysiology: Sensorimotor lacunar stroke is produced by occlusion of a small penetrating artery supplying the region where the ventral posterior thalamic nuclei lie immediately adjacent to the posterior limb of the internal capsule. A single lacune here simultaneously interrupts the crossed sensory pathways relaying through the thalamus and the descending corticospinal motor fibres in the capsule, yielding combined contralateral sensory loss and weakness affecting face, arm and leg. As with other lacunar strokes, the responsible arteriopathy is usually hypertensive lipohyalinosis or microatheroma of a deep perforating end-artery, producing a small cavitated infarct without involvement of the overlying cortex.
additionalDifferentials: Large-vessel cortical infarct with combined sensorimotor deficit
Pure motor hemiparesis or pure sensory stroke early in evolution
Space-occupying lesion compressing thalamus and capsule
Demyelinating lesion involving sensory and motor tracts
Postictal (Todd's) deficit after a focal seizure
additionalInvestigations: Diffusion-weighted and T2/FLAIR MRI of the brain
Non-contrast CT head to exclude deep haemorrhage
Carotid duplex and intracranial vascular imaging
ECG and extended cardiac rhythm monitoring
Fasting glucose, HbA1c and lipid profile
redFlags: Deteriorating conscious level or severe headache suggesting haemorrhage
Emergence of cortical signs indicating larger-territory infarction
Stuttering or crescendo progression of the deficit
New brainstem signs implying more extensive posterior-circulation ischaemia
reference.prognosis: Recovery is variable and often slower than in single-modality lacunar syndromes because both motor and sensory function are affected, though many patients still regain useful independence; recurrent small-vessel events and vascular cognitive decline remain important risks.
pitfalls: Mistaking a thalamocapsular haemorrhage for ischaemic lacunar stroke without imaging.
Classifying the event as cortical and pursuing unnecessary investigation when cortical signs are genuinely absent.
Assuming a normal early CT excludes infarction rather than proceeding to diffusion MRI.
Underestimating rehabilitation needs given the combined sensory and motor loss.
Failing to screen for a co-existent embolic source in a patient with small-vessel disease.
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Confirm ischaemia and exclude deep haemorrhage with urgent imaging, then offer intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase or tenecteplase to eligible patients within the treatment window
Start antiplatelet therapy with aspirin acutely, transitioning to long-term secondary prevention
Institute secondary prevention with a long-term antiplatelet agent and high-intensity statin
Control blood pressure with antihypertensive therapy as the key modifier of hypertensive small-vessel disease, alongside glycaemic control and smoking cessation
Begin early multidisciplinary rehabilitation with physiotherapy, occupational therapy, and sensory retraining for the combined motor and sensory deficit
Monitor for recurrent lacunar events and vascular cognitive decline, escalating to specialist stroke review as needed
